title: Kaizen and Zen
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of embracing life's experiences with an open and present mind, encouraging listeners to let go of expectations for rapid insight and instead cultivate a willingness to be vulnerable and kind through consistent practice. This approach is likened to the Japanese philosophy of Kaizen, which advocates for continuous improvement through small, daily actions that lead to gradual progress towards one's goals. By taking intentional steps each day, individuals can make meaningful changes in their lives and contribute to creating a better world around them.

sentences.text: My talk today will be about Zen and Kaizen, but I understand that nowadays it is expected that I open my talks with a poem.
For today, I have chosen Mary Oliver's poem, "Dogfish."
*Some kind of relaxed and beautiful thing kept flickering in with the tide and looking around.
Black as a fisherman's boot with a white belly.
If you asked for a picture, I would have to draw a smile under the perfectly round eyes and above the chin, which was rough, as a thousand sharpened nails.
And you know what a smile means, don't you?
I wanted the past to go away.
I wanted to leave it like another country.
I wanted my life to close and open like a hinge, like a wing, like the part of the song where it falls down over the rocks, an explosion, a discovery.
I wanted to hurry into the work of my life.
I wanted to know, whoever I was, I was alive for a little while.
It was evening and no longer summer.
Three small fish, I don't know what they were, huddled in the highest ripples as it came swimming in again, effortless.
The whole body, one gesture, one black sleeve that could easily fit around the bodies of three small fish.
Also, I wanted to be able to love.
And we all know how that one goes, don't we?
Slowly, the dogfish tore open the soft basins of water.
You don't want to hear the story of my life, and anyway, I don't want to tell it.
I want to listen to the enormous waterfalls of the sun.
And anyway, it's the same old story.
A few people just trying one way or another to survive.
Mostly, I want to be kind.
And nobody, of course, is kind or mean for a simple reason.
And nobody gets out of it, having to swim through the fires to stay in this world.
And look, look, look.
I think those little fish better wake up and dash themselves away from the hopeless future that is bulging toward them.
And probably, if they don't waste time looking for an easier world, they can do it.
So how are you doing today, my friends, on this beautiful day?
I hope that you are well and that your life is good.
What, you might ask, makes us stay beautiful?
Well, we woke up.
The rain is in the forecast when the sun rose behind the mountains.
It was a dark orange and the sky was flecked with clouds in so many colors and shapes.
Wind from the west rippled the water.
In the backyard, the apples are ripe and wild blackberries are juicy and sweet.
My chickens seem to be content.
They are off to explore the neighborhood.
But a beautiful day, perfectly perfect, in all its imperfection.
I am glad to be alive.
I'm glad to be here and to explore ideas together with you.
And I hope that you are willing to go on the exploration together with me because I might stray from what we usually consider as in some background.
Before I practiced Zen, I only had intellectual knowledge of it.
I read lots of books.
I fell in love with the idea of the sudden explosive insight demonstrated in koans.
I didn't think much more about it.
I thought that a monk would ask a question and the master would reply with a phrase or action that instantly burned away all uncertainty and clarified the great matter, satori.
What a fool I was.
I did not realize the thousand times the gateless gate had been opened for the monk before the great awakening.
I never considered that life in a Zen monastery in eighth century China was one of the most restricted and regulated environments imaginable.
And yet, great freedom came from exactly that source.
The moment of understanding that moving from conditioning to freedom is a tremendous change.
To be willing to step into the unknown, to be vulnerable and open in to a new territory.
Well, I was a fool in many ways and I guess I still am.
So, I think I joined the Bellingham Zen practice group in 2001.
Fortunately or unfortunately, it took me several months to figure out that there are two Zens, Soto and Rinzai.
And this group was Soto Zen.
Hint: Soto Zen does not work with koans in the way I had expected.
But by then it was too late and I was hooked.
I trust that I was very fortunate.
In my many years of practice, this explosive understanding that many people experience once or often has always escaped me.
I see that it's not my path.
Mine is sitting for many years and then at some point to discover that I have become kinder to the world and to myself.
That opposing facts can be true.
That having the upper hand does not mean winning.
That life is rich with love and that I can see Buddha in everyone.
So, Ryu Suzuki said this: After you have practiced for a while, you will realize that it is not possible to make rapid extraordinary progress.
Even though you may try very hard, the progress you make is always little by little.
It is not like going out in a shower in which you know when you get wet.
In a fog, you do not know you are getting wet.
But as you keep walking, you get wet little by little.
If your mind has ideas of progress, you may say, "Oh, this pace is terrible."
But actually, it is not.
When you get wet in the fog, it is very difficult to dry yourself.
So, there is no need to worry about progress.
This quote is from the book *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*.
Sometimes, I still have sentimental thoughts about satori.
However, that is being like a greedy child who cries for more sweets when both cheeks are already stuffed with candy.
Zazen, having a good teacher, being in Sangha, and studying the Dharma has changed my life and has made it so much sweeter.
Now, this will sound like a total change of subject, but I promise, or maybe I should say, I hope that it will all come together in the end.
So, some time ago, I ran into the concept Kaizen, K-A-I-Z-E-N.
It sounds very Zen, but has nothing to do with Zen practice or ritual.
Kaizen is a concept from post-World War II and was developed for industry and commerce.
It means continuous improvement.
Using Kaizen, great and lasting progress and success is achieved through small, consistent steps.
It turns out that slow and steady is the best way to overcome our resistance.
Slow and steady is the best way to overcome our resistance to change.
You cannot do Kaizen just once or twice and expect results.
You have to be in it for the long haul.
Small actions, repeated daily, are at the heart of Kaizen by taking steps so tiny that they seem trivial or even laughable.

You'll sail calmly past obstacles that may have defeated you before, because in absence of clearly defined goals, we may become strangely loyal to performing daily acts of trivia without thought, without a long-term game.
If you don't know where you are going, you might wind up somewhere else.
Part of the investigation is what, why, when, where, and who.
Any fixes and improvements you come up with will be applied in a dynamic way on the next day, no long-term planning required.
This dynamic is what fascinated me.
It challenges us to go from naive, just showing up and doing my thing, to deliberate.
And deliberate means getting out of the comfort zone, stretching the current skill, and then improving on it in a consistent manner.
The improved version becomes the new normal, which then in turn is approved upon.
It is the opposite of complacency.
Now Kaizen was definitely applied by Toyota, and we do know that for a long time, nobody could touch them in terms of workmanship.
But what can Kaizen look like when we are not Toyota?
What could it look like if we take it up as a personal practice?
What small step can I take today, right now, to improve, to move towards a life goal?
You may want to live at Tassajara for a practice period.
You may want to write a book.
I know at least one of you has.
You may want to get back to riding 100k on your bike.
My goal.
You may want to become a master chef or gardener, run a marathon, pick whatever you like, and then today, today, do something, even if it's laughably small, towards that goal.
Five minutes of zazen on chair.
Write 2,000 words.
Ride your bike around the block.
Put on your shoes and jog for two minutes.
Kaizen also means introspection, to see what happened while you engaged in the activity.
And most importantly, do something again on the next day to work towards your goal.
Kaizen is continued improvement and gradual continuous change.
The micro step of riding my bike around the block is fun.
But I couldn't do 100k right now.
Definitely not.
If you want to write a book, Stephen King, as we all know, is a prolific writer.
His goal is 2,000 words a day.
Every day.
So it's important to not break the chain.
Another thing is important.
The goals and the efforts need to be measurable and also not only the goal must be something clear and defined, but our daily efforts should be measurable too.
Time you're right around the block, try to go a little faster the next time.
So I think small actions like sitting zazen daily can lead to great changes.
And when it comes down to it, even our loftiest goals consist of many, many, many small manageable tasks.
So, I'm hoping that this talk can be a starting point for our conversation.
And if you're curious, there's lots of information available about Kaizen, because this talk doesn't even scratch the basics, doesn't even scratch the surface.
Even Dogen spoke about this continuous practice in his fascicle *Kyochi*, translation, "continuous practice."
And in his case, the continuous practice of discovering one's original face.
And I will end my talk with the beginning of the fascicle.
Beginning, ending, ending and beginning always was in the circle of the way.
The great road of Buddha ancestors, there is always unsurpassable practice, continuous and sustained.
It forms the circle of the way and is never cut off.
Between aspiration, practice, enlightenment and nirvana, there is not a moment's gap.
Continuous practice is the circle of the way.
This being so, continuous practice is undivided, not forced by you or others.
The power of this continuous practice confirms you as well as others.
It means your practice affects the entire earth and the entire sky in the ten directions.
Although not noticed by others or by yourself, it is so.
Accordingly, by the continuous practice of all Buddhas and ancestors, your practice is actualized and your great road opens up.
By your continuous practice, continuous practice of all Buddhas is actualized and the great road of all Buddhas opens up.
Your continuous practice creates the circle of the way.
By this practice, Buddha ancestors abide as Buddha, not abide as Buddha, have Buddha mind and attain Buddha without cutting off.
Because of this practice, there are the sun, the moon and stars.
Because of this practice, there are the great earth and the open sky.
Because of this practice, their body, mind and their environs.
Because of this practice, there are the four great elements and the five skandhas.
Continuous practice is not necessarily something people in the world love, but it should be the true place to return for everyone.
Because of the continuous practice of all Buddhas of the past, present and future, all Buddhas of the past, present and future are actualized.
